title: The deployment baseline
blurb: Define the deployment baseline, say what it contains and explain how it is used to measure and control delivery.
question: Eighteen weeks into building a school science block, the head teacher asks whether the project is 'on track'. What does the project manager measure progress against, and what has to happen if the head teacher then asks for an extra laboratory?

teach.body: The deployment baseline is the agreed, integrated plan of scope, schedule, cost, resources and quality against which deployment progress is measured and controlled. Plainly: it is the approved version of the plan that you hold the project to. Once it is approved, it is not quietly edited: any change to it goes through change control.

teach.caption: 'Integrated' means the elements are agreed as one set, so a change to one is checked for its effect on the others.

teach.h: Where the baseline is set in a linear life cycle
teach.caption: The baseline is agreed at the end of definition, at the decision gate into deployment, as part of the project management plan.

teach.body: Without a fixed reference you cannot say whether a project is ahead, behind or over budget. The baseline is the BASIS FOR PROGRESS MONITORING: actual performance is compared with it to reveal variances, forecast the outcome and trigger corrective action. It is also the REFERENCE POINT FOR CHANGE CONTROL: every change request is assessed for its impact against it. And it records what the sponsor and project manager agreed.

teach.h: Baseline vs actual: spotting a variance
teach.caption: Design overran by a week, so the forecast handover is a week later than the baseline. That gap is the variance the PM reports.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Kingsway School science block
teach.body: At the end of definition the sponsor approves the baseline: six laboratories (scope), 40 weeks (schedule), £3.2m (cost), the named contractor and in-house team (resources) and the building standards (quality). In week 18, the PM reports two weeks' slippage against the schedule baseline. The head teacher then asks for a seventh laboratory. That is a change request: it is assessed against the baseline and, if approved, the baseline is formally updated.

teach.caption: Only approved changes alter the baseline. Earlier versions are kept, so the history is clear.

rows.label: Approved scope, schedule, cost, resources and quality
Justification for investing in the project
Log of identified risks and their owners

teach.text: The deployment baseline is the basis for PROGRESS monitoring. Distractors describe it as the starting point for monitoring risks, the basis for an organisational breakdown structure or a resource histogram, or confuse it with the business case. None of these is right.

items: Deployment baseline: the agreed, integrated plan (scope, schedule, cost, resources, quality) that deployment progress is measured and controlled against.
Set and approved at the end of definition, before deployment starts.
Used to measure variance, forecast completion and assess change requests.
Once approved, it changes only through change control.

summary: You can now define the deployment baseline as the agreed, integrated plan that deployment progress is measured and controlled against, and name what it contains. You can explain when it is set, how variances are measured against it, and why changes to it must go through change control.

A.q: Which of the following best defines the deployment baseline?
options: The approved plan that progress is measured against
The first rough draft of the plan written at concept
The record of benefits tracked after handover
The list of risks to be monitored in delivery
A.why: The deployment baseline is the agreed, integrated plan against which deployment progress is measured and controlled.

whyNot.1: A first draft at concept is not approved and is far too early to be the baseline.
whyNot.2: Tracking benefits after handover is benefits management, not the baseline.
whyNot.3: A list of risks is the risk register, not the deployment baseline.

A.q: Which set of elements does a deployment baseline integrate?
options: Sponsor, project manager, team, users and PMO
Scope, schedule, cost, resources and quality
A.why: The baseline integrates scope, schedule, cost, resources and quality into one agreed plan.

whyNot.0: Benefits, risks and issues are managed through other processes and registers.
whyNot.1: These are project roles, not the contents of the baseline.
whyNot.3: These are PESTLE factors from the project environment.

A.q: Complete the statement: once the deployment baseline has been approved, any change to it must go through ____.
A.why: Change control captures, evaluates and approves, rejects or defers every request to change the approved baseline.

whyNot.0: The risk register records risks; it does not authorise changes to the baseline.
whyNot.1: A benefits review checks whether benefits are being realised.
whyNot.2: An audit gives independent assurance; it does not approve baseline changes.

B.q: At what point in a linear life cycle is the deployment baseline normally approved?
B.why: Detailed plans are built during definition, and the baseline is approved at the end of it, ready for deployment.

whyNot.0: At concept too little is known to fix a detailed baseline.
whyNot.2: Deployment is measured against the baseline, so it must exist before deployment starts.
whyNot.3: By transition the work is being handed over; it is far too late to set a baseline.

B.q: Four weeks into deployment, a project manager reports that spending is £40k higher than planned. What is this variance measured against?
B.why: Variance is the difference between actual performance and the deployment baseline.

whyNot.0: The business case compares options to justify the project; it is not used to measure delivery variance.
whyNot.1: The funnel shows how estimating accuracy improves; it is not a measure of progress.
whyNot.2: A stakeholder grid maps power and interest, not cost performance.

B.q: Why is the deployment baseline described as 'integrated'?
options: It is shared on the organisation's intranet
Its elements are agreed together as one
It merges the business case with the PMP
It integrates every lesson from past projects
B.why: Scope, schedule, cost, resources and quality are agreed as a single set, so a change to one is assessed against all the others.

whyNot.0: Where it is stored has nothing to do with it being integrated.
whyNot.2: The baseline forms part of the PMP but does not merge in the business case.
whyNot.3: Lessons from past projects may inform planning, but that is not what 'integrated' means.

C.q:
Which TWO of the following are purposes of a deployment baseline?
1) Providing the basis for progress monitoring
2) Justifying the investment to the board
3) Acting as the reference point for assessing changes
4) Recording lessons for future projects
C.why: The baseline is the basis for monitoring progress (1) and the reference against which change requests are assessed (3).

whyNot.0: Justifying the investment (2) is the job of the business case.
whyNot.1: Neither 2 nor 4 is a purpose of the baseline: those belong to the business case and lessons learned.
whyNot.3: Recording lessons (4) belongs to post-project review, not the baseline.

C.q: On the Kingsway project, the sponsor approves a change request to add a seventh laboratory. What should now happen to the deployment baseline?
options: It is left untouched as the original record
It is updated so progress is measured against it
It is discarded and a new business case written
It is replaced by the actual costs incurred so far
C.why: An approved change is built into a revised baseline, so future progress is measured against what has now been agreed. Earlier versions are kept for the record.

whyNot.0: If the baseline ignored an approved change, progress would be measured against an out-of-date plan.
whyNot.2: One approved change does not mean starting again; the baseline is revised, not discarded.
whyNot.3: Actual costs are compared with the baseline; they never replace it.

C.q: A project manager quietly updates the baseline every time the work slips, without any approval. What is the main problem with this?
options: Variances can no longer be seen or controlled
The estimating funnel will become wider again
The sponsor will lose ownership of the benefits
The critical path will automatically shorten
C.why: If the baseline moves with every slip, actual performance always matches it, so variances are hidden and control is lost. Changes need approval through change control.

whyNot.1: The funnel describes estimating accuracy; it is not affected by unapproved re-baselining.
whyNot.2: Benefits ownership stays with the sponsor regardless; the real damage is to visibility and control.
whyNot.3: Editing the baseline does not change the actual critical path of the work.

reteach.title: Building a house extension
reteach.question: You and your builder sign off drawings, a price and a 12-week programme for an extension. How is that agreement like a deployment baseline?

blocks.body: Before a brick is laid, you and the builder agree the drawings, the price, the 12-week programme, who is doing the work and the specification. Each week you check progress against that agreement. When you decide you want a skylight, the builder raises a variation: you agree the extra cost and time, and the agreement is updated. Nobody simply changes the drawings without asking.

blocks.text: Checking progress each week only works because there is an agreed plan to check against. That fixed reference is what makes a baseline useful.

explain.body: The deployment baseline is the agreed, approved plan for delivery. It is the yardstick: the fixed reference that deployment progress is measured and controlled against.

test.q: In plain English, what is the deployment baseline?
options: The team's list of open actions
test.why: It is the approved plan that delivery is measured and controlled against: a yardstick.

whyNot.1: The case for investing is the business case.
whyNot.2: A list of open actions is a working tool, not the baseline.
whyNot.3: The strategic plan sits at organisation level, above the project.

explain.body: The baseline integrates scope, schedule, cost, resources and quality. They are agreed together, because changing one, such as adding scope, usually affects the others.

test.q: Which of the following is NOT normally one of the elements fixed in a deployment baseline?
test.why: Stakeholder views are captured in stakeholder analysis; they are not an element of the baseline.

whyNot.0: Scope is a core element of the baseline.
whyNot.1: Cost is a core element of the baseline.
whyNot.3: Quality is part of the integrated baseline.

explain.body: In a linear life cycle the baseline is built during definition and approved at the decision gate into deployment, usually by the sponsor as part of approving the project management plan.

test.q: Who normally approves the deployment baseline before deployment begins?
options: The PMO at the end of deployment
The sponsor at the decision gate
test.why: The sponsor (often with the governance board) approves the plan and its baseline at the gate into deployment.

whyNot.0: The PMO supports and assures; it does not approve the baseline, and the end of deployment is too late.
whyNot.2: End users accept outputs at handover; they do not approve the baseline.
whyNot.3: A supplier agrees its own contract, not the project's baseline.

explain.body: During deployment, actual progress, cost and quality are compared with the baseline. The difference is the variance, which the PM reports and acts on. Proposed changes are assessed against the baseline through change control.

test.q: What does a project manager compare against the baseline to report variance?
test.why: Variance is found by comparing actual progress and cost with the baseline.

whyNot.1: Benefits are tracked through benefits management, not compared with the baseline to find delivery variance.
whyNot.2: The concept idea predates the baseline and is not a measure of progress.
whyNot.3: Strategy shapes why the project exists; it is not used to measure delivery variance.
